content: Routine vaccination of children has proven to be an effective strategy for reducing the incidence of hepatitis A in the United States. Since the introduction of the hepatitis A vaccine in 1995-1996, a phased approach to childhood immunization has been implemented. This began with the 1996 recommendation by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to vaccinate children in communities with the highest disease rates. By 1999, ACIP expanded its recommendations to include vaccination of children in states, counties, and communities with consistently elevated hepatitis A rates. The updated recommendations represent the final step in the nationwide childhood hepatitis A immunization strategy, advocating for routine vaccination of children across the country. Implementing these recommendations will strengthen existing vaccination programs, extend the benefits of hepatitis A vaccination to the entire nation, and lay the groundwork for potentially eliminating indigenous hepatitis A virus (HAV) transmission. This report updates ACIP's 1999 recommendations for preventing hepatitis A through immunization. It includes new epidemiological data on hepatitis A in the era of childhood vaccination in selected areas, results of economic analyses of nationwide routine vaccination, and recommendations for routine vaccination of children aged >1 year in the United States. Previous recommendations for vaccinating high-risk groups and the use of immune globulin for hepatitis A protection remain unchanged. Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a 27-nm RNA agent classified as a picornavirus. It can cause either asymptomatic or symptomatic infection in humans, with an average incubation period of 28 days (range: 15-50 days). Clinical illness caused by HAV typically has an abrupt onset, including symptoms such as fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice. The likelihood of symptomatic infection increases with age. In children aged <6 years, most infections are asymptomatic, and jaundice occurs in <10% of cases. In contrast, jaundice is observed in 70% of older children and adults. Symptoms usually last <2 months, but 10%-15% of symptomatic individuals may experience prolonged or relapsing illness for up to 6 months. Chronic infection does not occur, but persons with chronic liver disease are at increased risk for acute liver failure. HAV replicates in the liver, is excreted in bile, and is shed in stool. Peak infectivity occurs during the two weeks before the onset of jaundice or liver enzyme elevation, when the concentration of the virus in stool is highest. Viral shedding decreases after jaundice appears. Children can shed HAV for longer periods than adults, up to 10 weeks after the onset of clinical illness. Chronic shedding does not occur, but recurrent shedding can happen during relapses in individuals with relapsing illness. Viremia occurs soon after infection and persists through the period of liver enzyme elevation, although at much lower concentrations than in stool. Hepatitis A cannot be differentiated from other types of viral hepatitis based on clinical or epidemiologic features alone. Serologic testing to detect immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody to HAV (IgM anti-HAV) is required to confirm acute HAV infection. Sensitive tests for IgM and immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti-HAV in saliva have been developed but are not licensed in the United States. Serum IgM anti-HAV becomes detectable 5-10 days before symptom onset. IgG anti-HAV appears early in the infection and provides lifelong immunity. Two serologic tests are licensed for detecting HAV antibodies: IgM anti-HAV and total anti-HAV (IgM and IgG anti-HAV). In most patients, IgM anti-HAV declines to undetectable levels within one year after infection. HAV RNA can be detected in the blood and stool during the acute phase of infection using nucleic acid amplification methods. These methods have been used to determine the relatedness of HAV isolates for epidemiologic investigations, but only a limited number of research laboratories have the capacity to use these methods. Person-to-person transmission through the fecal-oral route is the primary mode of HAV transmission in the United States. Transmission occurs most frequently among close contacts, especially in households and extended family settings. Because most children have asymptomatic or unrecognized infections, they play a key role in HAV transmission and serve as a source of infection for others. Uncooked foods are frequently recognized as a source of outbreaks, while cooked foods can transmit HAV if cooking is inadequate or if contamination occurs after cooking, often involving infected food handlers. Waterborne outbreaks are infrequent in developed countries with well-maintained sanitation and water supplies. During 1980-1995, approximately 22,000-36,000 cases were reported annually to the CDC, but incidence models indicate that the number of infections was substantially higher. An estimated 271,000 infections occurred annually during 1980-1999, representing 10.4 times the reported number of cases. Each year, an estimated 100 persons died from acute liver failure attributed to hepatitis A. The costs associated with hepatitis A were substantial, with annual direct and indirect costs ranging from $300 million to $488.8 million in 1997 dollars. The introduction of the hepatitis A vaccine has led to a sharp decline in national hepatitis A rates. In 2004, a total of 5,683 cases were reported, representing an estimated 24,000 acute clinical cases when underreporting is considered. This rate was the lowest ever recorded and 79% lower than the previously recorded low in 1992. The decline is reflected in other fundamental shifts in hepatitis A epidemiology, including the narrowing or elimination of differences in age, race/ethnicity, and state-specific rates. These changes are largely attributed to the implementation of routine hepatitis A vaccination of children in states with historically elevated rates.
